# dev-prune (devp)

> A Rust CLI that reclaims disk space from idle Git repositories by deleting dependency
> and build directories — `node_modules`, `.venv`, `target`, `vendor` — but only after
> the project's own package manager confirms a lockfile can rebuild them. Apache-2.0,
> no analytics and no diagnostics; the only network request is an opt-out release
> check against GitHub. Windows, macOS, Linux.

Version 1.5.1. Written by VKrishna04.
Repository: https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune
Homepage: https://devprune.vkrishna04.me
JSON Schema for `.devprune.json`: https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/schemas/v1/devprune.schema.json

## What it is

`dev-prune` is the binary; `devp` is the same executable under a second name, and both
work in every shell. It registers Git repositories, judges each one idle from `git log`
commit timestamps *and* source file modification times, asks each package manager to
verify its lockfile, and only then deletes. `devp restore` puts everything back.

The core bet: a `node_modules` in a project you have not touched for weeks is a cache,
not data — the lockfile is the data. dev-prune deletes only what a lockfile can
provably regenerate, and treats "provably" literally: the package manager itself is run
in a read-only verification mode before anything is removed, and a verification that
fails, times out, or would need to rewrite the lockfile is a refusal.

## Why it exists / when to use it

- A development machine accumulates tens or hundreds of cloned repositories; each
  JavaScript project can hold 0.2–2 GB of `node_modules`, each Rust project multiple GB
  of `target`. Most are idle. dev-prune reclaims that space without deleting anything
  unrecoverable and without the user remembering which projects are safe.
- It runs unattended (OS scheduler + Git hooks that auto-register new clones), so the
  reclaiming keeps happening after the first run.
- Use `devp run --dry-run` to see what a pass would free; `devp status` for the
  interactive dashboard; `devp stats` for what has already been reclaimed over time.

When NOT to use it: it never deletes build *outputs* (`dist/`, `.next/`, compiled
artifacts) — those are not provably rebuildable from a lockfile and are permanently out
of scope. The one carve-out is the opt-in cargo/gradle/maven/swift adapters, whose build trees are
provably regenerated by recompiling the sources sitting next to them — and they stay
off until you switch them on. It is not a generic disk cleaner: directories outside registered Git
repositories are never touched. Machine-wide package caches are *reported* by
`devp caches` (with the vendor's own clear command) and never deleted by anything that
runs on its own, because a shared cache cannot be proven recoverable by any one lockfile
and it is what makes restore fast. `devp caches clear <manager>` empties one when you
type it, after showing what goes and asking.

## Install

- Linux, macOS, and Windows under Git Bash/MSYS2/Cygwin:
  `curl -fsSL https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/install.sh | sh`
- Windows PowerShell: `iwr -useb https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/install.ps1 | iex`
- Windows Command Prompt: `powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "iwr -useb https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/install.ps1 | iex"`
  (same install; `devp` resolves in the next Command Prompt, not the current one)
- Python tooling: `uv tool install dev-prune`, `uvx dev-prune status`,
  `pipx install dev-prune`, `pip install dev-prune`
- Cargo, prebuilt: `cargo binstall dev-prune`
- Cargo, from source: `cargo install dev-prune` (Rust 1.88+)
- Homebrew (macOS and Linux): `brew install Life-Experimentalist/tap/dev-prune`
  (the fully-qualified name taps as it installs; no separate `brew tap` step)
- Scoop (Windows): `scoop bucket add life-experimentalist https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/scoop-bucket`
  then `scoop install dev-prune`
- Homebrew and Scoop also install straight from a URL with nothing tapped or added:
  `brew install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/main/packaging/homebrew/dev-prune.rb`
  and `scoop install https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/main/packaging/scoop/dev-prune.json`

The Homebrew formula and the Scoop manifest are regenerated by the release itself from
the SHA-256 sidecars it just published, so both spellings always describe the newest
release and each one carries the hash of the archive it installs. The difference is
afterwards: a formula or manifest installed by URL belongs to no tap and no bucket, so
`brew upgrade` and `scoop update` never see a new version. The named tap
(`Life-Experimentalist/homebrew-tap`) and bucket (`Life-Experimentalist/scoop-bucket`)
exist for that, and each pulls its one file from `packaging/` in this repository daily.

`winget install VKrishna04.dev-prune` is submitted and awaiting review
(microsoft/winget-pkgs#422665); every winget-pkgs version is a pull request a person at
Microsoft signs off, so that command starts resolving when it merges and not before.
`brew install dev-prune` with no tap prefix means homebrew-core, which has a notability
bar and is not submitted.

## Editor integration

The companion extension is published as `VKrishna04.dev-prune` on the VS Code Marketplace
(https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=VKrishna04.dev-prune) and on Open VSX
(https://open-vsx.org/extension/VKrishna04/dev-prune), which covers VSCodium, Cursor,
Windsurf, Positron and Kiro. It validates `.devprune.json` from a schema bundled inside it
rather than fetched, and puts the workspace's reclaimable size in the status bar. Install
it with `code --install-extension VKrishna04.dev-prune`, or let `devp setup` offer it.

JetBrains IDEs need no extension: the config schema is registered with SchemaStore, so
IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, RubyMine, Rider, Visual Studio, Neovim and Zed
validate `.devprune.json` out of the box. `devp skill --agent <editor>` writes the rules
file a coding agent in that editor actually reads.

The PyPI packages contain the prebuilt binary rather than downloading one at install
time, so they install correctly behind a registry mirror and with no network access.
`cargo install` is the only channel that compiles on your machine — crates.io
distributes source, so there is no binary there for cargo to fetch. `cargo binstall`
reads the `[package.metadata.binstall]` table in `Cargo.toml` and downloads the GitHub
release archive instead, needing no toolchain.

Both installers take `--version`/`-Version`, `--bin-dir`/`-BinDir`, `--no-path`/`-NoPath`,
`--no-auto-setup`/`-NoAutoSetup` and `--help`/`-Help`. Piping into a shell has nowhere to
put an argument, so passing one means `… | sh -s -- --no-auto-setup` or
`& ([scriptblock]::Create((iwr -useb …))) -NoAutoSetup`; the equivalent environment
variables (`DEV_PRUNE_VERSION`, `DEV_PRUNE_BIN_DIR`, `DEV_PRUNE_NO_PATH=1`,
`DEV_PRUNE_NO_AUTO_SETUP=1`) work with the plain one-liner, and a flag wins over its
variable.

The installers verify the published SHA-256 checksum and refuse to install without one.
Seven prebuilt binaries cover everything: Windows, macOS and Linux on x64 and arm64,
plus a 32-bit windows-x86 build for machines with no 64-bit mode (there is no 32-bit
Linux, macOS or ARM build). The Linux builds are statically linked against musl, so there
is no per-distribution asset and no glibc floor — one file per architecture runs on
Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, Arch, NixOS and Alpine.

## Commands

- `devp init [PATHS]` — crawl for Git repositories and register them, then run the setup pass
- `devp link [PATH]` / `devp unlink [PATH]` — register or unregister one repository;
  `devp unlink --missing` drops every entry whose directory no longer exists
- `devp undo` — revert the most recent `init` or `link`
- `devp run [PATH]` — prune every registered repository, or one target
- `devp status [--top N] [--drift] [--json]` — interactive dashboard; a plain table when
  there is no TTY. In the dashboard `s` cycles the sort (relevance, size, longest idle,
  name), `f` cycles the filter (all, candidates, has bloat, problems) and `/` searches
  paths and adapter names; all three change only what is shown, never the totals. `--top N` lists only the N repositories with the most reclaimable
  space; the totals above the table still cover every registered repository. `--drift`
  replaces the dashboard with the lockfile-drift report: every environment holding
  packages its lockfile never recorded (`npm install --no-save`, a bare `pip install`
  into a pinned venv, an ad-hoc `uv pip install`), with the one command that records
  them — a pure read, and the same comparison a prune refuses on
- `devp stats [--json]` — what has already been reclaimed: lifetime total, prune passes,
  the most recent pass and how to undo it, and the repositories that gave back the most.
  Per-repository figures and the pass history are recorded from 1.1.0 onward
- `devp completions <bash|zsh|fish|powershell|elvish>` — print a shell completion script
  to stdout, generated from the same argument definition the binary parses with
- `devp caches [--json]` — find and size every package-manager cache and store on the
  machine (npm, pnpm, yarn, bun, uv, pip, cargo, go, maven, gradle, nuget, vcpkg, conan),
  largest first, with the command that clears each. The report deletes nothing, and no
  scheduler, Git hook or `devp run` ever will: a cache is shared by every project, so no
  one lockfile can prove it recoverable, and it is what makes `devp restore` fast. This is also where the
  .NET and C/C++ ecosystems are covered — their in-repository `bin/`+`obj/` and CMake
  `build/` directories are compiler outputs no lockfile can prove rebuildable, so
  dev-prune never deletes them, while their dependencies live in these machine-wide
  stores. Cargo `target/`, Maven `target/` and Gradle `build/`+`.gradle/` are the one
  exception, via the opt-in adapters below
- `devp caches clear <manager|all> [--dry-run] [--yes] [--json]` — empty one manager's
  cache, or every one of them, after listing and sizing what goes and asking. A
  convenience, never automation: only this command clears a cache, and only when you
  type it. It runs the manager's own subcommand wherever one exists (`npm cache clean
  --force`, `pnpm store prune`, `go clean -modcache`) because the manager knows what is
  still referenced; only cargo, maven, gradle and vcpkg, which ship nothing equivalent,
  are cleared by removing the directory this command already resolved and sized. A
  manager that is not installed is reported as failed, never deleted around. The freed
  size is measured afterwards rather than assumed. `--json` requires `--yes`; exit 1 if
  any cache could not be cleared, 2 for an unknown manager name
- `devp trust [--json]` — what dev-prune is allowed to do on this machine, on one
  screen. Two sections: the guarantees the code enforces on every machine (the seven
  safety invariants, no telemetry, build outputs never deleted — none with a setting or
  a flag behind it), and this machine read live (scheduler, Git hooks, registered
  repository count, idle window, managed binary path, and the four settings that widen
  anything: `auto_update`, `require_confirmation=false`, `allow_manifest_rewrite`, and
  any opt-in adapter: `enable_cargo`, `enable_gradle`, `enable_maven`,
  `enable_swift`, `enable_dart`). No letter grade — the widened settings are named, because
  "trust level: MEDIUM" tells nobody which switch to look at. Read-only, always exit 0
- `devp restore [PATH]` — reinstall dependencies for every project in a tree;
  `devp restore --last-run` restores exactly what the most recent prune pass deleted.
  A pruned virtual environment records the Python that built it and is rebuilt on that
  same interpreter; if it is no longer installed the restore asks once, defaults to no,
  and names the `uv python install` command that fixes it
- `devp doctor [PATH] [--fix]` — diagnose the installation, or one repository with a path
  (`devp doctor .` names the reason a prune pass would skip it); read-only, runs no
  package manager, repairs nothing. `devp doctor --fix` then repairs what the checks
  found, for installed-but-broken integrations only — a stale `devp` twin, hooks or a
  scheduler entry pointing at a binary that no longer exists, a drifted hook chain, a
  missing `SKILL.md` export, registry entries whose repository is gone. Each repair is
  the corresponding setup pass re-run, so it can never do more than `devp setup` would,
  and it never performs a first-time install
- `devp config …` — global settings, per-repo config, scheduler, hooks, file-manager icons;
  `devp config wizard` walks every setting and runs itself on the first install
- `devp setup [--status]` — install any missing integration; `--status` only reports
- `devp skill [--agent <editor>]` — export `SKILL.md` and install it into a detected
  agent skills directory (`~/.claude/skills/dev-prune/`); prints onboarding prompts for
  agents without one. `--agent` writes per-repository rules for one editor instead.
  Ten write a file of their own: cursor (`.cursor/rules/dev-prune.mdc`), windsurf
  (`.windsurf/rules/`), antigravity (`.agent/rules/`), cline (`.clinerules/`), roo
  (`.roo/rules/`), kilocode (`.kilocode/rules/`), continue (`.continue/rules/`),
  amazon-q (`.amazonq/rules/`), kiro (`.kiro/steering/`) and trae (`.trae/rules/`).
  Five share a file with other tools and get a marked block inside it: agents-md
  (`AGENTS.md`, read by Codex, Jules, Amp and OpenCode), copilot
  (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`), gemini (`GEMINI.md`), junie
  (`.junie/guidelines.md`) and zed (`.rules`)
- `devp update [--offline | --install]` — print the installed version, check GitHub for a newer release, and show the upgrade command. `--install` downloads the release binary for this platform from GitHub Releases, refuses it unless its SHA-256 matches the published sidecar, and writes it to every copy this installation runs: the managed binary under the config directory, its `devp` alias, the windowless `devpw` scheduler twin, and the running binary. The package manager that delivered the first copy is deliberately not run — its version record goes stale and the single command that resyncs it is printed — and its own upgrade command is the fallback when no binary is published for this platform or the download fails. `devp config set auto_update true` runs it by itself after a prune pass; an upgrade never interrupts the scheduler. `DEV_PRUNE_OFFLINE=1` in the environment keeps the process off the network entirely, regardless of any setting
- `devp man [--dir <dir>]` — the manual as man pages, generated from the same clap
  definitions `--help` uses. Alone: the `devp(1)` page to stdout (pipe into `man -l -`);
  `--dir` writes the full set, one page per subcommand
- `devp uninstall [--deep]` — remove the program: scheduler, hooks, agent skill, PATH
  entry and the binaries themselves, then a sweep over PATH and the well-known install
  dirs (`~/.cargo/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, npm global, venv Scripts) removes every other
  copy after one confirmation (`-y` covers it; non-interactive without `-y` skips the
  sweep with a note). Manager-owned copies get the exact uninstall line printed so the
  manager's records clear too; `--deep` also clears config
- `devp -V` — version plus an environment audit

Global flags: `--dry-run`, `--ignore-idle` (`--force` is the deprecated alias),
`-y`/`--yes`, `--json` on the reporting commands (`run`, `status`, `stats`, `trust`, `caches`).
Piped `--json` output is one document on stdout and nothing else; only when stdout is
an actual terminal is the document also copied to the human's clipboard (stderr note).
`devp run --except <name>` prunes everything *but* the named repositories, which is the
usual way to keep one project warm. `devp run --only <adapter>` / `--skip <adapter>`
narrow a pass to named ecosystems. `devp run --explain` lists every repository and
directory with the reason it would or would not be pruned — including the states a
normal pass keeps quiet about (still active, opted out, under the size floor);
read-only, and it conflicts with `--json`. A `.` for `[PATH]` means the current directory and
is accepted everywhere a path is.

Exit codes are a contract: `0` success, `1` failure (a run in which any repository
failed exits `1` even if others succeeded), `2` unusable arguments. `devp doctor` exits
`0` for warnings and `1` only for genuine breakage.

## The seven safety invariants

Enforced in code, with no bypass flag — full detail with the exact commands in
https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/blob/main/docs/SAFETY_INVARIANTS.md:

1. **`.git` boundary** — nothing outside a directory containing a `.git` folder is ever
   processed. Linked worktrees and submodule checkouts (a `.git` *file*) are refused,
   conservatively.
2. **Lockfile pre-verification** — before deletion, the ecosystem's manager runs a
   read-only check (`npm ci --dry-run --ignore-scripts`,
   `pnpm install --lockfile-only --frozen-lockfile`,
   `bun install --frozen-lockfile --dry-run --ignore-scripts`, `uv lock --locked`,
   `cargo metadata --locked`, `go mod download`, …) under a timeout. If the manager is
   missing but a lockfile exists, the lockfile itself is the proof. A drifted lockfile
   is a refusal, not something to quietly fix: rewriting forms
   (`cargo generate-lockfile`, `go mod tidy`, …) run only when no lockfile exists at
   all, or after the explicit opt-in `devp config set allow_manifest_rewrite true`.
   The venv adapter runs nothing: it requires `requirements.txt` to list at least one
   package and refuses when the environment holds packages the file never recorded.
3. **Idleness** — `max(last commit, newest source mtime)` must be older than
   `idle_days` (default 15). `--ignore-idle` lifts this check and nothing else.
4. **Atomic state writes** — the registry is written to a temp file and renamed, never
   edited in place; a crash mid-write leaves the previous state intact.
5. **Opt-outs** — `ignore.devprune.json` in a repository root is honoured by file
   presence alone (0 ms, nothing parsed); `"ignore": true` in `.devprune.json` does the
   same after a parse. A `.devprune.json` that does not parse skips the repository and
   reports the error — defaults are never guessed for a file that said something.
6. **Symlink refusal** — a bloat directory that is a symlink or Windows junction points
   at storage the repository does not own (typically a monorepo's real `node_modules`)
   and is refused, never followed. The directory walk never follows links either.
7. **Nested-repository boundary** — discovery walks at most `scan_depth` levels
   (default 6, max 32), never descends into `node_modules`/`target`/`vendor`/venvs or
   hidden directories, and never crosses into a nested `.git` repository — a submodule
   or vendored checkout has its own history and is pruned only in its own right.

Also deliberate: `--dry-run` verifies nothing (it reports sizes and stops before
verification, which is why it is instant), and `.devprune.json` holds inert data only —
no key in it can name a command to run or a path to delete, because the file arrives
with a `git clone` of possibly-untrusted code.

## What it never does

- Never deletes build outputs (`dist/`, `.next/`, `bin/`+`obj/`, compiled artifacts) —
  no lockfile proves them rebuildable.
- Never deletes a machine-wide cache on its own. `devp caches` reports them with each
  vendor's own clear command, and `devp caches clear` empties one only when you type it —
  no scheduler, Git hook or prune pass ever touches one.
- Never executes anything named in a repository-tracked file.
- Never rewrites a lockfile during verification, by default in every ecosystem.
- Never edits editor settings, `PATH`, or shell startup files; for editors it prints a
  snippet you paste yourself.
- Never phones home: no analytics, no telemetry; the single network request is the
  opt-out update check against GitHub's public API (no body, no identifier).

## Supported ecosystems

Twenty adapters. npm, pnpm, yarn, bun (`node_modules`); uv, poetry, pdm, pipenv and
pip/venv (`.venv`, `__pypackages__`, any directory holding `pyvenv.cfg`); go
(`vendor`); composer (`vendor`); bundler (`vendor/bundle`); cocoapods (`Pods`); mix
(`deps`); terraform (`.terraform/providers`); and, opt-in, cargo (`target/`), gradle
(`build/`, `.gradle/`), maven (`target/`), swift (`.build/`) and dart (`.dart_tool/`).
The build-tool adapters ship disabled — a build tree is regenerated by recompiling, not
downloading, so they cost more to get back: `devp config set enable_cargo true` /
`enable_gradle true` / `enable_maven true` / `enable_swift true` / `enable_dart true`
turns them on, and their candidates wait for `build_idle_days`
(45 by default, applied as the maximum of it and `idle_days`). `adapter_idle_days`
(`cargo=90,npm=30`) raises one named adapter's window further still, never lowering it. .NET and C/C++ are covered by `devp caches` (their
dependencies live in machine-wide stores; their in-repo build directories are outputs,
see above).

Bundler and pipenv claim only the install that lives inside the repository: the
`vendor/bundle` that follows `bundle config set path vendor/bundle`, and the `.venv`
that appears under `PIPENV_VENV_IN_PROJECT`. Both tools default to a shared store under
the user's home directory, which dev-prune never touches — neither as a prune nor
through `devp caches`, because that directory is where other projects' dependencies are
installed rather than a cache. Composer declines `vendor/` entirely when a
`vendor/bundle` is inside it, because no `composer install` puts those gems back. Mix
takes `deps/` and never `_build/`; swift takes `.build/` and never `.swiftpm/`; dart
takes `.dart_tool/` and never `build/`. Terraform takes `.terraform/providers` and
nothing else under `.terraform/` — `environment` records the selected workspace and
losing it silently returns you to `default`, `terraform.tfstate` is the backend's
initialisation record, and `modules/` comes from sources the lock file says nothing
about.

cocoapods, mix, dart, terraform, gradle, maven and swift verify offline: their ecosystems have no
read-only in-sync command, and the write-side ones fix drift by re-downloading, so what
is checked is that the lockfile is structurally complete and no older than the manifest
it came from, or that the build manifest the tree is derived from is present and parses.

Any of the eighteen can be switched off with `disabled_adapters`.

A repository may hold any number of these, at the root or up to `scan_depth` levels
below it. Where several managers claim the same `node_modules`, the owner is chosen
from the `packageManager` field, else the bookkeeping files inside the installed tree,
else the most recently written lockfile. uv wins over plain venv when `uv.lock` or
`[tool.uv]` is present.

Sizing is honest about hardlinks (1.1.0): under pnpm and bun, files hardlinked into the
manager's global store are excluded from the reported reclaimable size — deleting
`node_modules` removes the link but the store keeps the bytes. The excluded amount is
reported separately (`shared_bytes` in `--json`). Copied installs (exFAT, cross-volume
stores, macOS clonefile) count in full. The prune itself always removes the whole
directory; hardlink awareness changes accounting, never what is deleted.

## Configuration

Global settings live in `%APPDATA%\dev-prune` (Windows),
`~/Library/Application Support/dev-prune` (macOS), `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dev-prune` (Linux).
Twenty-three keys, all readable with `devp config get <key>` and writable with
`devp config set <key> <value>`: `idle_days` (15), `min_size_mb` (0), `scan_depth` (6),
`require_confirmation` (true), `allow_manifest_rewrite` (false),
`command_timeout_secs` (600), `auto_setup` (true), `auto_config` (false),
`auto_daemon` (true), `check_interval_days` (2), `auto_hooks` (true),
`auto_hooks_chain` (false), `update_check` (true), `update_check_interval_days` (7),
`update_check_timeout_secs` (5), `enable_cargo` (false), `enable_gradle` (false),
`enable_maven` (false), `enable_swift` (false), `enable_dart` (false),
`build_idle_days` (45),
`adapter_idle_days` (none), `auto_update` (false), `disabled_adapters` (none).

`disabled_adapters` is a comma-separated list of adapter names to leave alone
entirely: a disabled adapter is not detected, not counted by `stats`, not probed for
by `doctor` and never pruned, as if that ecosystem were not installed on the machine.
`devp config set disabled_adapters -` clears it. It is a deny-list rather than
twenty switches because the answer for almost everyone is "none", and it is
separate from `enable_cargo` / `enable_gradle` / `enable_maven` / `enable_swift` /
`enable_dart`,
which are off because of what their directories cost to rebuild rather than because
anyone dislikes them.

`devp config wizard` opens all twenty-four in a full-screen configurator — the
`devp trust` declaration first, then every setting, then a summary of exactly what
will be written. It runs itself once on a first install and again after an upgrade
adds a setting the machine has never been shown, marking that one `NEW`; settings
already confirmed are never re-asked. `--no-tui` or `DEV_PRUNE_NO_TUI=1` asks one
question per line instead. Agents should use `devp config set`, which needs no
terminal at all.

Per repository: `ignore.devprune.json` in the root is an instant opt-out;
`.devprune.json` supports `project_name`, `ignore`, `disable_daemon`, `disable_hooks`,
and the three overrides `override_idle_days`, `min_size_mb`, `scan_depth`. Files
written by `devp config project` carry a `$schema` link, and the schema is published at
https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/schemas/v1/devprune.schema.json for editor IntelliSense.
The other global settings have no per-repository form deliberately — nothing stops a
project from committing its `.devprune.json`, so a repository must not be able to grant
itself `allow_manifest_rewrite`. Both files hold inert data only.

## Machine-readable output (for tools and AI agents)

Add `--json` to `run`, `status`, `stats`, `trust` or `caches` for a versioned JSON document
(`schema` 1, additive changes only within a major version). Highlights:

- `devp status --json` — per-repository totals, per-directory sizes, and status
  (candidate / active / ignored / no_bloat / path_missing / config_error).
- `devp run --json` — one result per repository × directory with the action taken or
  the refusal reason; refusals include the exact fix command where one exists
  (e.g. the lockfile-repair command for that ecosystem). `size_freed` counts only bytes
  deletion actually returns; `shared_bytes` is what hardlinked stores keep.
- Exit codes carry meaning (see above), so scripting on them is supported.

For AI coding assistants there is a dedicated skill file:
`devp skill` exports it locally, and the canonical copy is
https://github.com/Life-Experimentalist/dev-prune/blob/main/.agents/skills/dev-prune/SKILL.md
— a task-to-command table (including "is this safe?" answers), the JSON field
reference, and the failure playbook. Agents should prefer `--json` over parsing the
human report, use `--dry-run` before a destructive suggestion, and never suggest
`--ignore-idle` without asking the user first.

## Background automation

The `devp` second binary, the managed binary directory on `PATH` (a user `PATH` entry
on Windows, `~/.local/bin` symlinks elsewhere — this is what keeps a pip-in-venv
install working after the venv is gone), the exported `SKILL.md`, the skill installed
into any detected agent skills directory, global Git auto-registration hooks,
the OS scheduler and the file-manager icons install themselves at install time, and
again on `devp init` or after an upgrade if any of them is missing. `devp setup` runs
the same pass by hand and `devp setup --status` only reports. Hooks are skipped when
`git` is not on `PATH`. When the global `core.hooksPath` already belongs to husky,
pre-commit or lefthook, the pass skips the hooks and says so; `devp hook install --chain`
takes the slot and writes shims that `exec` the displaced directory's same-named hook,
so both run. An unchained install shims every hook name too, forwarding to the
repository's own `.git/hooks`, so setting `core.hooksPath` does not disable a repo-local
pre-commit gate. Chaining is opt-in — `auto_hooks_chain` defaults to false. Turn any of it
off with `auto_setup`/`auto_hooks`/`auto_hooks_chain`/`auto_daemon`, or
`DEV_PRUNE_NO_AUTO_SETUP=1` in the environment. Everything the setup pass writes lives
under your own config and data directories and is removed by `devp uninstall`.

## Guides

Long-form answers to the questions that lead people here, at
https://devprune.vkrishna04.me/blog/ :

- /safe-to-delete-node-modules/ — is it safe to delete `node_modules`, and how to check
- /delete-node-modules-all-projects/ — clearing `node_modules` across a whole machine
- /reclaim-disk-space-developer-machine/ — where a developer machine's disk actually goes
- /clear-package-manager-cache/ — the right clear command for thirteen managers
- /delete-venv-safely/ — deleting `.venv` for uv, Poetry, PDM, Pipenv and plain venv
- /cargo-target-directory-size/ — why Rust's `target/` grows, and what to delete
- /vs/ — an honest comparison with npkill, cargo-sweep, rimraf and a cron job
